The Mariana swiftlet Aerodramus bartschi is a small, cave-nesting apodid endemic to the Mariana archipelago, where its life history is shaped by the stable thermal conditions of its subterranean roosts. Neonates emerge from the incubated bird egg with a wet body mass of approximately 1.11 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.11 grams], a value typical of altricial hatchlings among the swiftlets. This modest birth mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the developing chick, which must rely entirely on parental provisioning from the moment of hatching. Under the relatively constant temperatures maintained within the limestone caverns that this species frequents, embryo development proceeds at an average incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], which yields a total age at birth of about 23 days [ab = about 23 days]. This incubation period is comparable to that of other Aerodramus species, suggesting a conserved developmental tempo within the genus that is finely tuned to the thermal microenvironment of the nest chamber.

The exponential growth phase of the nestling chick is remarkably rapid, driven by intensive biparental provisioning of insect prey gathered during foraging flights. Hatchlings advance from their initial wet weight of just over one gram to the ultimate wet weight attained by fully developed juveniles approaching fledging. Field records indicate that asymptotic mass for nestlings reaches 8.21 grams [Wwi = 8.21 grams], a figure that closely matches the average adult body weight of 8.01 grams reported for free-living individuals. This near-equivalence between fledgling mass and adult mass suggests that chicks complete the bulk of their somatic growth during the nestling stage, leaving relatively little to be gained after departure from the nest. The energetic demands of this rapid mass increase are substantial, requiring parents to deliver hundreds of prey items daily during the peak of the brooding period, especially when the growing juvenile bird experiences the elevated metabolic costs typical of endothermic development.

This delay is thought to reflect the high energetic investment required to reach the asymptotic body mass before reproductive activation can occur, as well as the competitive demands of securing a nesting site within the crowded cave colonies. The first successful breeding event for Aerodramus bartschi typically occurs at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], exactly one full year after the individual's own emergence from the egg at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This precise annual cycle aligns with the species' strictly seasonal reproductive schedule, which is entrained by the availability of flying insect prey during the wet season. The decision to invest in a single offspring per breeding attempt reflects the high energy cost of provisioning a rapidly growing nestling over an extended brooding period, as well as the limited number of safe nesting cavities available within the cave environment. The close synchronization of first reproduction with the one-year anniversary of birth ensures that young breeders enter the nesting population at the optimal time of year for maximizing offspring survival.

This relatively prolonged nestling period, exceeding six weeks, is unusual among birds of such small body size and underscores the slow developmental tempo of the species. Maximum recorded longevity for the Mariana swiftlet, estimated from banding studies and extrapolated from congeneric data for the common swift Apus apus, reaches approximately 7702 days [am = approximately 7702 days], or just over 21 years under the same thermal conditions. Such an extraordinarily long lifespan for a 8-gram bird is a classic correlate of a low annual reproductive output and high adult survival, hallmarks of a life history strategy adapted to the stable but resource-limited environment of tropical island caves.
